svg.title: Commander AI decision: one group per pass of $6564
svg.desc: Flow of the commander AI's group loop $6564 and decision chain $65b4 with the natural hit count of each arm. Sources (reversing/powermonger/strategy.md): "The commander AI `$6522`" (the filters, the state switch, decide arms 1 to 5, "The pending word"), "Natural coverage" (short census 95 / 2 / 77 / 179 / 137; 75-land census $65c8 3507, $65f4 2286, $6638 31122, $666c 145, $668c 5, $664c 6913, $66a4 0, $6884 0), "The exact arm conditions" (predicate_check.py 5724/5724), "Food fallback `$66a4`" (food_boundary.py 15/15), "Transfer `$664c`, `$668c`", "Refusal `$6884` cannot hold from any caller", "Proof of the commander AI" (gate_cmdai.py 323/323 natural, 280/280 synthetic). Branch addresses checked against a disassembly of $6564..$66e6 (scratchpad/pm123/win/m1_map.ram). Full fact list: cmdai_decision.facts.md.
svg.text: How the computer's commander AI picks one order for one army group
Blue numbers = how often each branch fired in a test of 75 random lands; "short" marks a smaller test (29 saved games, 150M steps each).
proven (checked against the game's own code)
observed (seen in the running game)
inferred (read from the code, not run)
PowerMonger (Bullfrog / Electronic Arts, 1990, here the Atari ST version) is a war game in which the player and the computer lords
command armies through captains. This figure comes from reverse-engineering the game's 68000 machine code (the ST's CPU) and running it
in an emulator. Each side has six captains' groups. Once per tick, the game's simulation step, the commander AI ($6522) looks for one
group of a computer side to give an order. Its loop ($6564) walks the groups from 5 down to 0, skips any that does not exist or already
has an order in flight (an order still travelling to its captain by carrier pigeon), and runs the decision chain ($65b4) for the first
group that is free to act.
The chain is a fixed priority list, first match wins: fetch men when the group is small, escort the first captain's group when it is
fighting, march on the nearest enemy lord when the group has the food for the trip, and a few rarer arms (an arm is one branch of the
list). Apart from a short follow-up table there is no planning: with the men's own state machines (see the two mode figures), this page
is the whole autonomous AI.
$ numbers are addresses in the game's memory, given as citations; the text says what each one is. Evidence: proven = checked against the game's own code
with a match count; observed = seen in the running game; inferred = read from the code or reasoned, not run.

Whole routine: matched on 323/323 natural and 280/280 constructed states. Arm conditions (predicates): 5724/5724.
75-land test: 75 unmodified Play Random Land lands x 2G steps (about 78G steps with the land alive).
Short test: 29 saved start states x 150M steps. The 6913 at $664c are mostly group 0 and empty groups re-deciding every tick.
Natural transfers and the land-143 arm-4 decision: 6/6 states, 28/28 changed bytes against the game's own routine ($6522).

svg.text: How to read it
Read top to bottom; each box on the left is a test and each box on the right an outcome. The top part filters: an arrow to the right leaves the chain
without a decision. A group in state 9 (deciding) goes straight to the decide part along the line on the left; a group in state 6 (camped) first
waits 20 ticks after its camp stamp and then tries the follow-up table, which chains food, men, equipment and invention orders after a finished
state. In the decide part the left boxes are the arm conditions in the order the code tests them; the first that holds sends the group to the box on
its right. That box gives the posture the AI writes into the group (its aggression setting: 2 aggressive, 3 neutral, 4 passive) and the order it
issues: $08 get men, $0c march and engage, $06 get food, $04 transfer men, $02 from the target recheck. The blue number under an arm is how often it
fired in the 75-land test.
Takeaway: the computer's whole strategy is a short priority list that mostly marches on the nearest enemy lord (the attack arm fired 31122 times in
the test, against 3507 for get-men and 2286 for the escort); the food fallback and the refusal never fired, and the transfer fired 5 times in 75
lands. AI groups start with $5fff food, so the attack arm's food test never stops an AI attack in any run. The AI writes posture 4 (passive) on every
group it sends to attack, which turns every kill in a fight into a rout, so its attacks scatter armies rather than kill them.
Terms and evidence
Proven: the routine was rewritten in Python and run beside the game's own 68000 code, called in isolation from saved game states with the emulator's
callcap command (which runs one routine from a saved state and records what it changed); it matched every changed byte on 323 of 323 states captured
in natural play and 280 of 280 constructed ones. Observed: hit counts at each arm's address while lands play with no input. Play Random Land is the
game's option that builds a random land; "land 25" and the like are such lands. Steps are emulated instructions (M a million, G a thousand million).
The n(A1) and n(group) terms are fields of the group record: 4 the pending-order word, 28 owner side, 52 men, 76 state, 112 food, 136 posture, 256
camp stamp, 268 previous state, 280 opponent class (the group-field figure maps them). $69b4 finds an own lord, $68fe an enemy lord, $68ee scores the
trip.
Sources: strategy.md "The commander AI $6522", "Natural coverage", "The exact arm conditions", "Food fallback $66a4", "Transfer $664c, $668c", "Refusal $6884", "Proof of the
commander AI", "Data structures (C)" (the $30fe comment) and "What's crude, and what a modern version changes" (item 6: posture 4 forces every kill into a rout); scripts
py/cmdai/gate_cmdai.py, py/arms/predicate_check.py, py/arms/summarize.py (75-land test, runs L2G and M2G), py/cmdai/census.py (short test), py/arms/gate_nat_arms.py,
py/arms/food_boundary.py; the lands are named k25, k143, k106, k50, k8, k34 in the run files; cmdai_decision.facts.md.
